Speeding up PCA imputation

Source: vignettes/articles/speeding-up-pca-imputation.qmd 
library(slideimp)

pca_imp() does the PCA imputation in slide_imp(), tune_imp(), and group_imp() when they impute with PCA. This article shows how to make PCA imputation faster with the threshold, scale, and solver arguments, and with a parallel backend from mirai.

Before you tune anything, run pca_imp() with .progress = TRUE on a meaningful subset of the variables, for example chromosome 22, to see how fast it runs. Ctrl+C stops a run before it ends.

Arguments that set the speed

For large numeric matrices, three arguments can reduce the runtime by a large amount: threshold, scale, and solver.

set.seed(1234) # simulate some data
sim <- sim_mat(
  n = 80,
  p = 1500,
  rho = 0.7,
  perc_total_na = 0.10,
  perc_col_na = 0.8
)
sim_df <- sim$col_group
obj <- sim$input

threshold

threshold is the convergence threshold of the PCA imputation algorithm. The default, threshold = 1e-6, matches the conservative behavior of missMDA. For many genomic matrices, threshold = 1e-5 is much faster and gives very similar imputed values.

scale

The columns are always centered before PCA, and scale sets whether they are also scaled to unit variance. The default scale = TRUE adds work to every iteration. For data with columns on the same scale, such as DNAm beta values in [0, 1], scale = TRUE can amplify columns with low variance and columns that are mostly noise. For such data, scale = FALSE can be both faster and more accurate.

solver

solver takes three values: two PCA eigensolvers, and "auto", which chooses between them:

  • solver = "exact" uses an exact solver. It always converges, and it is typically faster for small to moderate matrices.
  • solver = "lobpcg" uses an iterative eigensolver with warm starts. It can be faster for large, approximately low-rank matrices with a small ncp, especially when the imputation needs many EM iterations.
  • solver = "auto", the default, uses "exact" for small problems. For other problems, it runs a short timed probe of both solvers and picks "lobpcg" only when it is clearly faster.

solver = "auto" is a good default for most users. Set solver to "exact" or "lobpcg" when:

  • You run many independent pca_imp() calls, for example in tune_imp() or group_imp(). Each call can run its own probe, and the probes add time.
  • You know which solver is faster on your data, and "auto" picks the other one.

If neither solver is clearly faster on a representative subset, pick solver = "exact", because it always converges.

Tuning workflow

The best settings depend on the hardware, the BLAS library, the matrix size, and the missing-data pattern. Before an expensive analysis, tune pca_imp() in these steps:

  1. Choose a representative subset of the data, for example chromosome 22.
  2. Time the exact and lobpcg solvers on the subset at a fixed threshold.
  3. Use tune_imp() to check that a relaxed threshold and scale = FALSE do not materially change the cross-validation error.
  4. Fix solver, threshold, and scale, then tune the other parameters (ncp and coeff.ridge, and window_size and overlap_size for slide_imp()).

Create a representative test matrix

In a real DNA methylation analysis, use a representative chromosome or subset. Here, group1 of the simulated data stands in for that chromosome.

set.seed(12345)

obj_probe <- obj[, subset(sim_df, group == "group1")$feature]

dim(obj_probe)
#> [1]  80 731
mean(is.na(obj_probe))
#> [1] 0.09849521

Time the solvers

Use a small ncp and a relaxed threshold = 1e-5 for the timing. This ncp does not have to be the final ncp. Both solvers use the same convergence criterion, so their relative timing is representative.

Run this timing on your own representative subset. On the simulated data of this article, the two solvers take a similar time, so the chunk below is not run here. A positive difference means that "lobpcg" was faster.

ncp_probe <- 5
exact <- system.time(invisible(
  pca_imp(
    obj = obj_probe,
    ncp = ncp_probe,
    solver = "exact",
    threshold = 1e-5
  )
))

iterative <- system.time(invisible(
  pca_imp(
    obj = obj_probe,
    ncp = ncp_probe,
    solver = "lobpcg",
    threshold = 1e-5
  )
))

# diff
exact[["elapsed"]] - iterative[["elapsed"]]

Check threshold

Use tune_imp() to compare the cross-validation error across threshold values. In this example, the error at 1e-5 is very close to the error at 1e-6.

thresh_df <- data.frame(threshold = c(1e-5, 1e-6), ncp = ncp_probe)
res <- tune_imp(obj = obj_probe, parameters = thresh_df, .f = "pca_imp")
#> Tuning `pca_imp()`
#> Step 1/2: Resolving NA locations
#> Using default `num_na` = 500 (~0.85% of cells).
#> ℹ Increase `num_na` for more stable metrics, or decrease it when `obj` already
#>   has many missing values.
#> Running mode: sequential
#> Step 2/2: Tuning

compute_metrics(res)
#>   threshold ncp param_set rep_id error   n n_miss .metric .estimator  .estimate
#> 1     1e-05   5         1      1  <NA> 500      0     mae   standard 0.09335752
#> 2     1e-05   5         1      1  <NA> 500      0    rmse   standard 0.11652556
#> 3     1e-06   5         2      1  <NA> 500      0     mae   standard 0.09320836
#> 4     1e-06   5         2      1  <NA> 500      0    rmse   standard 0.11641720

Check scale

scale = FALSE can be faster and more accurate for some DNAm data, but it is not always more accurate. Compare its error against the default with tune_imp(). tune_imp() does not report the time, so time the two settings as in the solver timing above.

scale_df <- data.frame(
  scale = c(TRUE, FALSE),
  ncp = ncp_probe,
  threshold = 1e-5
)
res_scale <- tune_imp(obj = obj_probe, parameters = scale_df, .f = "pca_imp")
#> Tuning `pca_imp()`
#> Step 1/2: Resolving NA locations
#> Using default `num_na` = 500 (~0.85% of cells).
#> ℹ Increase `num_na` for more stable metrics, or decrease it when `obj` already
#>   has many missing values.
#> Running mode: sequential
#> Step 2/2: Tuning

compute_metrics(res_scale)
#>   scale ncp threshold param_set rep_id error   n n_miss .metric .estimator
#> 1  TRUE   5     1e-05         1      1  <NA> 500      0     mae   standard
#> 2  TRUE   5     1e-05         1      1  <NA> 500      0    rmse   standard
#> 3 FALSE   5     1e-05         2      1  <NA> 500      0     mae   standard
#> 4 FALSE   5     1e-05         2      1  <NA> 500      0    rmse   standard
#>    .estimate
#> 1 0.08928488
#> 2 0.11088626
#> 3 0.08957511
#> 4 0.11124100

In this example, the error with scale = FALSE is very close to the error with the default, and slightly higher.

Tune accuracy parameters with the chosen settings

After you choose solver, threshold, and scale, keep them fixed while you tune the accuracy arguments ncp and coeff.ridge. On the simulated data here, the two solvers take a similar time, so this example keeps "exact". On a large, approximately low-rank matrix that needs many EM iterations, "lobpcg" with warm starts is typically faster. The example also uses scale = FALSE, because its error is very close to the default and scale = FALSE can be faster.

chosen_solver <- "exact"
chosen_threshold <- 1e-5
chosen_scale <- FALSE

# tune ncp and coeff.ridge
params <- expand.grid(
  ncp = c(2, 4, 6),
  coeff.ridge = c(0.8, 1, 1.2)
)

params$solver <- chosen_solver
params$threshold <- chosen_threshold
params$scale <- chosen_scale

tune_pca <- tune_imp(
  obj = obj_probe,
  .f = "pca_imp",
  parameters = params,
  n_reps = 1 # <- increase to a higher number in real analyses
)
#> Tuning `pca_imp()`
#> Step 1/2: Resolving NA locations
#> Using default `num_na` = 500 (~0.85% of cells).
#> ℹ Increase `num_na` for more stable metrics, or decrease it when `obj` already
#>   has many missing values.
#> Running mode: sequential
#> Step 2/2: Tuning

metrics <- compute_metrics(tune_pca, metrics = "rmse")

aggregate(
  .estimate ~ ncp + coeff.ridge,
  data = metrics,
  FUN = mean
)
#>   ncp coeff.ridge .estimate
#> 1   2         0.8 0.1124445
#> 2   4         0.8 0.1128692
#> 3   6         0.8 0.1133943
#> 4   2         1.0 0.1122923
#> 5   4         1.0 0.1125142
#> 6   6         1.0 0.1127536
#> 7   2         1.2 0.1121828
#> 8   4         1.2 0.1122631
#> 9   6         1.2 0.1123292

Apply to slide_imp()

The same steps apply to sliding-window PCA imputation. slide_imp() typically works on small windows, each with few columns, so solver = "exact" is usually a good default. With solver = "auto", the first window that completes the solver probe picks the solver, and every later window uses it.

beta_matrix <- obj_probe # Treat `obj_probe` as a `slide_imp()` input
locations <- seq_len(ncol(beta_matrix))
slide_params <- expand.grid(
  ncp = c(2, 4),
  coeff.ridge = c(0.8, 1, 1.2),
  window_size = c(50, 500) # Adjust based on units of `locations`
)

slide_params$overlap_size <- 5
slide_params$min_window_n <- 20
slide_params$solver <- "exact" # Usually better for `slide_imp()`
slide_params$threshold <- chosen_threshold
slide_params$scale <- chosen_scale

tune_slide_pca <- tune_imp(
  obj = beta_matrix,
  .f = "slide_imp",
  parameters = slide_params,
  n_reps = 1, # <- increase to a higher number in real analyses
  location = locations
)
#> Tuning `slide_imp()`
#> Step 1/2: Resolving NA locations
#> Using default `num_na` = 500 (~0.85% of cells).
#> ℹ Increase `num_na` for more stable metrics, or decrease it when `obj` already
#>   has many missing values.
#> Running mode: sequential
#> Step 2/2: Tuning

slide_metrics <- compute_metrics(tune_slide_pca, metrics = "rmse")

aggregate(
  .estimate ~ ncp + coeff.ridge + window_size,
  data = slide_metrics,
  FUN = mean
)
#>    ncp coeff.ridge window_size .estimate
#> 1    2         0.8          50 0.1111740
#> 2    4         0.8          50 0.1162099
#> 3    2         1.0          50 0.1106076
#> 4    4         1.0          50 0.1147531
#> 5    2         1.2          50 0.1104182
#> 6    4         1.2          50 0.1134466
#> 7    2         0.8         500 0.1107731
#> 8    4         0.8         500 0.1134791
#> 9    2         1.0         500 0.1104863
#> 10   4         1.0         500 0.1126640
#> 11   2         1.2         500 0.1102355
#> 12   4         1.2         500 0.1119397

Finally, impute with the selected parameters. Here the call runs on beta_matrix, the group1 subset. In a real analysis, pass the full matrix:

slide_results <- slide_imp(
  obj = beta_matrix,
  location = locations,
  window_size = 500,
  overlap_size = 5,
  min_window_n = 20,
  ncp = 2,
  coeff.ridge = 1.2,
  solver = "exact",
  threshold = chosen_threshold,
  scale = chosen_scale,
  .progress = FALSE
)

Parallel PCA imputation and BLAS threading

tune_imp() and group_imp() can also make PCA imputation faster by running independent imputation tasks in parallel on mirai daemons. Their cores argument applies to K-NN imputation only.

When PCA imputation runs in parallel, each daemon can call multithreaded linear algebra routines through BLAS. If each daemon uses several BLAS threads, the total number of active CPU threads can far exceed the number of physical cores. For example, 8 mirai daemons that each use 8 BLAS threads request 64 threads. This thread oversubscription can make code slower rather than faster.

group_imp() and tune_imp() prevent this by default: pin_blas = TRUE uses RhpcBLASctl to limit BLAS to one thread on each daemon. On Linux, this works with common BLAS libraries such as OpenBLAS, FlexiBLAS, and MKL. Set pin_blas = FALSE to let each daemon use a threaded BLAS, for example when a few daemons run on many cores.

On Windows, with OpenBLAS in place of R’s own BLAS, pin_blas = TRUE does not limit every BLAS and LAPACK call that PCA imputation makes. To keep each daemon on one thread, set OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 before R starts, for example in .Renviron. Or do not start mirai daemons, so the tasks run in sequence, and let the multithreaded OpenBLAS use the cores.

library(mirai)

mirai::daemons(4)

pca_group_results <- group_imp(
  obj = obj,
  group = sim_df,
  ncp = 2,
  solver = chosen_solver,
  threshold = chosen_threshold,
  scale = chosen_scale
)
#> Imputing 2 groups using PCA.
#> Running mode: mirai

mirai::daemons(0)
